# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Overview

This repo is **hasToggle.dev** — the unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel. The product is `apps/web`: a lab of chapters that each open on a belief a developer holds and run the real feature next to it. See `README.md` for the shape of the lab and where the chapter code lives.

The monorepo around it was scaffolded from [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge) (`npx next-forge init` — a one-time copy, no upstream, no shared history). It uses Bun workspaces and Turborepo. The other apps and most of `packages/*` came with the scaffold and are not part of the site.

## Development Commands

### Setup & Installation
```bash
bun install                    # Install all dependencies
```

Set `MONGODB_URI` in the environment (validated via @t3-oss/env-nextjs in `packages/database/keys.ts`).

### Running Applications
```bash
bun dev                       # Run all apps in development mode
turbo dev --filter=app         # Run only the main app (port 3000)
turbo dev --filter=web         # Run only the web/marketing site (port 3001)
turbo dev --filter=api         # Run only the API (port 3002, includes Stripe webhook listener)
```

### Testing
```bash
bun test                      # Run tests across all workspaces
turbo test --filter=app        # Run tests for specific app
bun test                       # Run Bun test runner in apps/app or apps/api
```

### Code Quality
```bash
bun run check                     # Run Biome linter/formatter checks (uses ultracite presets)
bun run fix                       # Auto-fix linting/formatting issues
turbo boundaries               # Check package boundaries
```

### Building
```bash
bun run build                     # Build all apps (depends on tests passing)
turbo build --filter=app       # Build specific app
turbo analyze --filter=app     # Analyze bundle size
```

### Database

The database is MongoDB, accessed through the official `mongodb` driver — there is no ORM, no schema migrations, and no generated client. `packages/database/index.ts` exports a `database` object with typed collection handles; document types live in `packages/database/types.ts`.

### Maintenance
```bash
bun run bump-deps                 # Update dependencies (excludes recharts)
bun run bump-ui                   # Update shadcn/ui components
bun run clean                     # Clean node_modules from root
turbo clean                    # Clean build artifacts and node_modules from all workspaces
```

## Architecture

### Monorepo Structure

The repository uses **Bun workspaces** with two main directories:

- **apps/** - Deployable applications (independently deployable)
- **packages/** - Shared packages consumed by apps

### Applications (apps/)

1. **app** (port 3000) - Main SaaS application
   - Authentication via better-auth (route groups: `(authenticated)` and `(unauthenticated)`); handler mounted at `/api/auth/[...all]`
   - Uses Next.js 16 with App Router
   - Server actions in `app/actions/`
   - API routes in `app/api/`
   - Tests configured with Bun test runner

2. **web** (port 3001) - Marketing/landing page
   - Internationalization support (uses `[locale]` route)
   - Content management via CMS package
   - Rate limiting via Arcjet

3. **api** (port 3002) - RESTful API server
   - Health check endpoint at `/health`
   - Webhook handlers in `app/webhooks/`
   - Cron jobs in `app/cron/`
   - Development includes Stripe webhook listener (requires Stripe CLI)

4. **email** - Email templates (React Email)
5. **storybook** (`apps/storybook`) - Component development environment.
   Its package name is `@repo/storybook`, **not** `storybook`: Bun links every
   workspace package into the root `node_modules` by name, so a workspace named
   `storybook` shadows the real `storybook` npm package and every addon that
   imports `storybook/internal/*` fails to resolve. Turbo filter is
   `--filter=@repo/storybook`. Never name a workspace after one of its own
   dependencies.
6. **studio** - Database management UI (stale Prisma Studio wrapper; non-functional since the MongoDB migration)

### Shared Packages (packages/)

Core infrastructure packages:

- **@repo/auth** - better-auth authentication (client, server, middleware, provider)
  - MongoDB adapter + organization plugin; the active org id is the tenant id
  - Server instance in `instance.ts`; `server.ts` is a Clerk-shaped compat layer
    (`auth()`, `currentUser()`) so callers did not have to change
  - Handler mounted by apps/app at `/api/auth/[...all]`
- **@repo/database** - MongoDB via the official `mongodb` driver (server-only)
  - Typed collection handles exported from `packages/database/index.ts`
  - Document types at `packages/database/types.ts`
  - Requires `MONGODB_URI` (validated in `packages/database/keys.ts`)
- **@repo/design-system** - shadcn/ui component library
  - Components in `components/` (auto-generated, excluded from Biome linting)
  - Providers for themes, tooltips, etc.
  - Dark mode support via next-themes
- **@repo/observability** - Sentry error tracking and logging
- **@repo/security** - Arcjet integration for application security
- **@repo/analytics** - Google Analytics and PostHog
- **@repo/payments** - Stripe integration
- **@repo/email** - Resend email service
- **@repo/webhooks** - Webhook handling (inbound/outbound)
- **@repo/collaboration** - Real-time features (Liveblocks)
- **@repo/feature-flags** - Feature flag management
- **@repo/notifications** - In-app notifications
- **@repo/internationalization** - i18n support
- **@repo/cms** - Content management (BaseHub)
- **@repo/seo** - SEO utilities
- **@repo/storage** - File upload/management
- **@repo/ai** - AI integration utilities

### Technology Stack

Exact versions live in the `package.json` files and drift with every Renovate
run — read them there. Majors are named below only where they change how you
write code.

- **Framework**: Next.js 16 with App Router, React 19
- **Language**: TypeScript 7 — the native Go compiler, not the old JS one.
  Strict mode, NodeNext module resolution. See below.
- **Package Manager**: Bun (pinned via `packageManager`)
- **Build Tool**: Turborepo
- **Database**: MongoDB via the official `mongodb` driver
- **Auth**: better-auth (email/password + organizations)
- **Styling**: Tailwind CSS
- **Linting**: Biome with ultracite presets (core, react, next)
- **Testing**: Bun test runner
- **Bundling**: none for `packages/*` — apps consume them as TypeScript source
  through the `workspace:*` protocol

#### TypeScript 7

`typescript` is a thin Node wrapper around a native Go binary. It ships **no
JavaScript compiler API** — `typescript/lib/typescript.js` does not exist, and
only the `typescript/unstable/*` entry points are available. Any tool that
expects to `require("typescript")` and build a `Program` will fail here; that
is a constraint on dependency choices, not a bug to fix.

Type safety is gated twice:

- `next build` type-checks each app by spawning the `tsc` CLI
  (`experimental.useTypeScriptCli`, on by default since Next.js 16.3).
- The turbo `typecheck` task runs native `tsc --noEmit` everywhere, which is
  what covers `packages/*` — `next build` never sees those. `build` depends
  on it.

### Important Patterns

1. **Workspace Dependencies**: Internal packages use `workspace:*` protocol
   - Example: `"@repo/auth": "workspace:*"`

2. **Route Groups**: Apps use Next.js route groups for layout separation
   - app: `(authenticated)` and `(unauthenticated)` groups
   - web: `[locale]` for internationalization

3. **Server/Client Separation**: Packages use `server-only` for server-side code
   - Database and auth server utilities are server-only
   - Client components/utilities are separate files

4. **Environment Variables**: Uses @t3-oss/env-nextjs for type-safe env validation

5. **Path Aliases**: Apps configure aliases via tsconfig.json paths
   - `@/` - points to app root
   - `@repo/` - points to packages directory

6. **Biome Exclusions**: Auto-generated code excluded from linting:
   - `packages/design-system/components/ui` (shadcn components)
   - `packages/collaboration/config.ts` (Liveblocks config)
   - `packages/cms/basehub-types.d.ts` (CMS types)

7. **Build Dependencies**: `turbo.json` configures build to depend on tests passing
   - Builds run `^build` (dependency builds) then `test` before building

## Key Files

- `turbo.json` - Turborepo task pipeline configuration
- `biome.jsonc` - Linter/formatter configuration (extends ultracite presets)
- `packages/database/types.ts` - Database document types
- `docs/voice.md` - The writing voice for anything a visitor reads
- `docs/design.md` - The instrument design grammar for the playground demos
- Root `package.json` - Monorepo scripts and workspace configuration (private; nothing here is published)
- `scripts/skip-ci.js` - The Vercel "Ignored Build Step" every app's `vercel.json` points at

## Writing copy

Any user-facing prose in `apps/web` or `packages/email` — exhibit titles, demo
prose, asides, panel labels, FAQ answers, digest copy — follows `docs/voice.md`.
Read it before drafting, and edit against its three passes (§5) before calling
copy done. It is short on purpose; do not skim it.

Do not add rules to it casually. A rejected line that an existing rule already
predicted means the guide worked and needs no edit — see §9.

## Designing demos

Demo UI follows `docs/design.md` — the fixed instrument grammar (state gauge,
view controls, specimen, deck, reference bar), the feedback rules, and the
current migration state. Read it before building or reshaping an exhibit.
Copy and demo co-evolve: when a panel gains a capability, re-run voice.md's
three passes over the exhibit's prose, because the instrument may have
obsoleted lines that were accurate when they shipped.

Design rounds in this repo run on proposals: present options with a clear
recommendation and the trade-offs named, get an explicit yes, then build.
Project knowledge belongs in the repo — these docs, not external notes.

## Development Notes

- The main branch is not explicitly configured in git - PRs should target the default branch
- Apps have independent dev ports: app (3000), web (3001), api (3002)
- API development automatically runs Stripe CLI webhook forwarding to localhost:3002/webhooks/payments
- MongoDB access goes through the shared client in `packages/database/index.ts` (cached on `global` in development to survive hot reloads)
- Tests and typechecks must pass before builds complete (enforced by Turborepo pipeline)
- The design system excludes shadcn auto-generated UI components from version control linting

[Next.js Docs]
STOP. What you remember about Next.js is WRONG for this project. Read the docs before any Next.js task.
The full, version-matched docs ship inside the installed package: `apps/web/node_modules/next/dist/docs/` — markdown mirroring nextjs.org/docs (`01-app/01-getting-started/`, `01-app/02-guides/`, `01-app/03-api-reference/`, `02-pages/`, `03-architecture/`). Search there with grep/glob; there is no `.next-docs` directory in this repo. The `nextjs_docs` MCP tool (next-devtools) returns this same path.

- [Eric's background](user_eric.md) — Developer-educator, cognitive science + M.Ed., Pratchett-style preferences
- [hasToggle positioning](project_hastoggle_positioning.md) — 2026-07 pivot: live playground for Next.js/Vercel, cohort+digest funnel, voice layers kept
- [Brainstorming and design rounds](feedback_brainstorming.md) — Options + clear recommendation + named trade-offs; short approvals; four-audience test; engineer-not-student
- [Playground design language](project_playground_design_language.md) — Pointer to docs/design.md; Eric's rule: hasToggle knowledge lives in-repo, structured
- [Don't commit specs/plans](feedback_no_commit_artifacts.md) — On landing-page-rewrite, spec + plan markdown stays untracked
- [Commit regularly by default](feedback_commit_regularly.md) — Verified unit done = commit it, don't wait to be asked

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Overview

This repo is **hasToggle.dev** — the unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel. The product is `apps/web`: a lab of chapters that each open on a belief a developer holds and run the real feature next to it. See `README.md` for the shape of the lab and where the chapter code lives.

The monorepo around it was scaffolded from [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge) (`npx next-forge init` — a one-time copy, no upstream, no shared history). It uses Bun workspaces and Turborepo. The other apps and most of `packages/*` came with the scaffold and are not part of the site.

## Development Commands

### Setup & Installation
```bash
bun install                    # Install all dependencies
```

Set `MONGODB_URI` in the environment (validated via @t3-oss/env-nextjs in `packages/database/keys.ts`).

### Running Applications
```bash
bun dev                       # Run all apps in development mode
turbo dev --filter=app         # Run only the main app (port 3000)
turbo dev --filter=web         # Run only the web/marketing site (port 3001)
turbo dev --filter=api         # Run only the API (port 3002, includes Stripe webhook listener)
```

### Testing
```bash
bun test                      # Run tests across all workspaces
turbo test --filter=app        # Run tests for specific app
bun test                       # Run Bun test runner in apps/app or apps/api
```

### Code Quality
```bash
bun run check                     # Run Biome linter/formatter checks (uses ultracite presets)
bun run fix                       # Auto-fix linting/formatting issues
turbo boundaries               # Check package boundaries
```

### Building
```bash
bun run build                     # Build all apps (depends on tests passing)
turbo build --filter=app       # Build specific app
turbo analyze --filter=app     # Analyze bundle size
```

### Database

The database is MongoDB, accessed through the official `mongodb` driver — there is no ORM, no schema migrations, and no generated client. `packages/database/index.ts` exports a `database` object with typed collection handles; document types live in `packages/database/types.ts`.

### Maintenance
```bash
bun run bump-deps                 # Update dependencies (excludes recharts)
bun run bump-ui                   # Update shadcn/ui components
bun run clean                     # Clean node_modules from root
turbo clean                    # Clean build artifacts and node_modules from all workspaces
```

## Architecture

### Monorepo Structure

The repository uses **Bun workspaces** with two main directories:

- **apps/** - Deployable applications (independently deployable)
- **packages/** - Shared packages consumed by apps

### Applications (apps/)

1. **app** (port 3000) - Main SaaS application
   - Authentication via better-auth (route groups: `(authenticated)` and `(unauthenticated)`); handler mounted at `/api/auth/[...all]`
   - Uses Next.js 16 with App Router
   - Server actions in `app/actions/`
   - API routes in `app/api/`
   - Tests configured with Bun test runner

2. **web** (port 3001) - Marketing/landing page
   - Internationalization support (uses `[locale]` route)
   - Content management via CMS package
   - Rate limiting via Arcjet

3. **api** (port 3002) - RESTful API server
   - Health check endpoint at `/health`
   - Webhook handlers in `app/webhooks/`
   - Cron jobs in `app/cron/`
   - Development includes Stripe webhook listener (requires Stripe CLI)

4. **email** - Email templates (React Email)
5. **storybook** (`apps/storybook`) - Component development environment.
   Its package name is `@repo/storybook`, **not** `storybook`: Bun links every
   workspace package into the root `node_modules` by name, so a workspace named
   `storybook` shadows the real `storybook` npm package and every addon that
   imports `storybook/internal/*` fails to resolve. Turbo filter is
   `--filter=@repo/storybook`. Never name a workspace after one of its own
   dependencies.
6. **studio** - Database management UI (stale Prisma Studio wrapper; non-functional since the MongoDB migration)

### Shared Packages (packages/)

Core infrastructure packages:

- **@repo/auth** - better-auth authentication (client, server, middleware, provider)
  - MongoDB adapter + organization plugin; the active org id is the tenant id
  - Server instance in `instance.ts`; `server.ts` is a Clerk-shaped compat layer
    (`auth()`, `currentUser()`) so callers did not have to change
  - Handler mounted by apps/app at `/api/auth/[...all]`
- **@repo/database** - MongoDB via the official `mongodb` driver (server-only)
  - Typed collection handles exported from `packages/database/index.ts`
  - Document types at `packages/database/types.ts`
  - Requires `MONGODB_URI` (validated in `packages/database/keys.ts`)
- **@repo/design-system** - shadcn/ui component library
  - Components in `components/` (auto-generated, excluded from Biome linting)
  - Providers for themes, tooltips, etc.
  - Dark mode support via next-themes
- **@repo/observability** - Sentry error tracking and logging
- **@repo/security** - Arcjet integration for application security
- **@repo/analytics** - Google Analytics and PostHog
- **@repo/payments** - Stripe integration
- **@repo/email** - Resend email service
- **@repo/webhooks** - Webhook handling (inbound/outbound)
- **@repo/collaboration** - Real-time features (Liveblocks)
- **@repo/feature-flags** - Feature flag management
- **@repo/notifications** - In-app notifications
- **@repo/internationalization** - i18n support
- **@repo/cms** - Content management (BaseHub)
- **@repo/seo** - SEO utilities
- **@repo/storage** - File upload/management
- **@repo/ai** - AI integration utilities

### Technology Stack

Exact versions live in the `package.json` files and drift with every Renovate
run — read them there. Majors are named below only where they change how you
write code.

- **Framework**: Next.js 16 with App Router, React 19
- **Language**: TypeScript 7 — the native Go compiler, not the old JS one.
  Strict mode, NodeNext module resolution. See below.
- **Package Manager**: Bun (pinned via `packageManager`)
- **Build Tool**: Turborepo
- **Database**: MongoDB via the official `mongodb` driver
- **Auth**: better-auth (email/password + organizations)
- **Styling**: Tailwind CSS
- **Linting**: Biome with ultracite presets (core, react, next)
- **Testing**: Bun test runner
- **Bundling**: none for `packages/*` — apps consume them as TypeScript source
  through the `workspace:*` protocol

#### TypeScript 7

`typescript` is a thin Node wrapper around a native Go binary. It ships **no
JavaScript compiler API** — `typescript/lib/typescript.js` does not exist, and
only the `typescript/unstable/*` entry points are available. Any tool that
expects to `require("typescript")` and build a `Program` will fail here; that
is a constraint on dependency choices, not a bug to fix.

Type safety is gated twice:

- `next build` type-checks each app by spawning the `tsc` CLI
  (`experimental.useTypeScriptCli`, on by default since Next.js 16.3).
- The turbo `typecheck` task runs native `tsc --noEmit` everywhere, which is
  what covers `packages/*` — `next build` never sees those. `build` depends
  on it.

### Important Patterns

1. **Workspace Dependencies**: Internal packages use `workspace:*` protocol
   - Example: `"@repo/auth": "workspace:*"`

2. **Route Groups**: Apps use Next.js route groups for layout separation
   - app: `(authenticated)` and `(unauthenticated)` groups
   - web: `[locale]` for internationalization

3. **Server/Client Separation**: Packages use `server-only` for server-side code
   - Database and auth server utilities are server-only
   - Client components/utilities are separate files

4. **Environment Variables**: Uses @t3-oss/env-nextjs for type-safe env validation

5. **Path Aliases**: Apps configure aliases via tsconfig.json paths
   - `@/` - points to app root
   - `@repo/` - points to packages directory

6. **Biome Exclusions**: Auto-generated code excluded from linting:
   - `packages/design-system/components/ui` (shadcn components)
   - `packages/collaboration/config.ts` (Liveblocks config)
   - `packages/cms/basehub-types.d.ts` (CMS types)

7. **Build Dependencies**: `turbo.json` configures build to depend on tests passing
   - Builds run `^build` (dependency builds) then `test` before building

## Key Files

- `turbo.json` - Turborepo task pipeline configuration
- `biome.jsonc` - Linter/formatter configuration (extends ultracite presets)
- `packages/database/types.ts` - Database document types
- `docs/voice.md` - The writing voice for anything a visitor reads
- `docs/design.md` - The instrument design grammar for the playground demos
- Root `package.json` - Monorepo scripts and workspace configuration (private; nothing here is published)
- `scripts/skip-ci.js` - The Vercel "Ignored Build Step" every app's `vercel.json` points at

## Writing copy

Any user-facing prose in `apps/web` or `packages/email` — exhibit titles, demo
prose, asides, panel labels, FAQ answers, digest copy — follows `docs/voice.md`.
Read it before drafting, and edit against its three passes (§5) before calling
copy done. It is short on purpose; do not skim it.

Do not add rules to it casually. A rejected line that an existing rule already
predicted means the guide worked and needs no edit — see §9.

## Designing demos

Demo UI follows `docs/design.md` — the fixed instrument grammar (state gauge,
view controls, specimen, deck, reference bar), the feedback rules, and the
current migration state. Read it before building or reshaping an exhibit.
Copy and demo co-evolve: when a panel gains a capability, re-run voice.md's
three passes over the exhibit's prose, because the instrument may have
obsoleted lines that were accurate when they shipped.

Design rounds in this repo run on proposals: present options with a clear
recommendation and the trade-offs named, get an explicit yes, then build.
Project knowledge belongs in the repo — these docs, not external notes.

## Development Notes

- The main branch is not explicitly configured in git - PRs should target the default branch
- Apps have independent dev ports: app (3000), web (3001), api (3002)
- API development automatically runs Stripe CLI webhook forwarding to localhost:3002/webhooks/payments
- MongoDB access goes through the shared client in `packages/database/index.ts` (cached on `global` in development to survive hot reloads)
- Tests and typechecks must pass before builds complete (enforced by Turborepo pipeline)
- The design system excludes shadcn auto-generated UI components from version control linting

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

input.prompt: Summarize exactly how Resend supports unsubscribe for transactional (API-sent) emails: List-Unsubscribe / List-Unsubscribe-Post headers, whether Resend auto-adds them, use of topic_id / topics on emails.send, {{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}} availability outside broadcasts, what happens to the contact when a recipient uses Resend's hosted unsubscribe (unsubscribed flag vs deletion vs suppression), and any preference page / one-click behavior. Quote key sentences.

content.content:
# Resend Transactional Email Unsubscribe Support

Based on the documentation provided, here's how Resend handles unsubscribe for transactional emails:

## Manual Header Implementation Required
Resend does **not automatically add** unsubscribe headers. You must manually include them: "you can add the `List-Unsubscribe: https://example.com/unsubscribe` header when sending emails using the Resend API."

## RFC 8058 Compliance (Required for Bulk Senders)
For messages exceeding 5,000 daily sends, you must implement: "a URL version in your list-unsubscribe header, `List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click`, and to allow for a `POST` request."

## Server-Side Requirements
Your endpoint must handle both:
- **POST requests:** Return blank page with 200/202 status
- **GET requests:** Display regular unsubscribe page

"Ensure that users stop receiving email within 48 hours of this request."

## Key Limitations
- **No automatic contact management:** "Resend doesn't manage contact lists for transactional emails."
- **No mention of:** topic_id, {{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}} tokens, or hosted unsubscribe pages for transactional mail
- **For managed unsubscribe workflows:** The documentation redirects to Audiences/Broadcasts, not transactional APIs

The documentation does not detail what happens to contact records post-unsubscribe (suppression vs. deletion).

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

content.content:
# Resend Topics: Key Behaviors

## Email Sending with topic_id
The documentation doesn't explicitly detail what Resend adds to email headers when `topic_id` is specified via API. However, it confirms topics enable scoped sending and unsubscribe preferences.

## Unsubscribe Link & Preference Page
When contacts click an unsubscribe link in a broadcast, they reach a preference page offering two choices:

> "Unsubscribe from certain **Topics** (types of email) / Or unsubscribe from **everything** you send"

Selecting a topic opt-out removes them from that category only. Choosing full unsubscription prevents all broadcasts.

## Contact Requirement
The documentation doesn't address whether contacts must pre-exist before sending with `topic_id`. This detail isn't covered in the provided content.

## Global vs. Topic-Level Unsubscribe
A critical distinction exists:

> "The **Subscribed** status is a global setting that enables or disables sending to a Contact for Broadcasts."

A false global "Subscribed" status blocks all emails, regardless of topic preferences. Topic opt-outs are granular; > "they will no longer receive emails for those Topics."

## State Changes on Unsubscribe
The documentation describes unsubscribe behavior but doesn't clarify whether this sets an "unsubscribed flag" or only modifies topic preferences. It implies topic opt-out modification occurs.

## Webhooks
No webhook events are mentioned in this documentation excerpt.

### Batch Email Parameters

Source: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/emails/send-batch-emails

Details on the request parameters available when sending emails via the Resend API.

```APIDOC
## Email Request Parameters

### Parameters

#### Request Body
- **headers** (object) - Optional - Custom headers to add to the email.
- **topic_id** (string) - Optional - The topic ID to receive the email. If the recipient is a contact and has opted-in to the topic, the email is sent. If opted-out, the email is not sent. If not a contact, the email is sent if the topic default subscription is 'opt-in'.
- **tags** (array) - Optional - Custom data passed in key/value pairs.
  - **name** (string) - Required - The name of the email tag (ASCII letters, numbers, underscores, or dashes, max 256 chars).
  - **value** (string) - Required - The value of the email tag (ASCII letters, numbers, underscores, or dashes, max 256 chars).
- **template** (object) - Optional - Configuration for sending via a template.
  - **id** (string) - Required - The id or alias of the published template.
  - **variables** (object) - Optional - An object with a key for each variable.

### Notes
- If a `template` is provided, you cannot send `html`, `text`, or `react` in the payload.
- When sending a template, `from`, `subject`, and `reply_to` in the payload take precedence over template defaults.
```

--------------------------------

### Update Contact Topics via cURL

Source: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/contacts/update-contact-topics

Perform a PATCH request to the Resend API to update contact topics by ID or email.

```bash
// Update by contact id
curl -X PATCH 'https://api.resend.com/contacts/e169aa45-1ecf-4183-9955-b1499d5701d3/topics' \
     -H 'Authorization: Bearer re_xxxxxxxxx' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d $'[
      {
        "id": "b6d24b8e-af0b-4c3c-be0c-359bbd97381e",
        "subscription": "opt_out"
      }
     ]'

// Update by contact email
curl -X PATCH 'https://api.resend.com/contacts/[REDACTED_EMAIL]/topics' \
     -H 'Authorization: Bearer re_xxxxxxxxx' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d $'[
      {
        "id": "b6d24b8e-af0b-4c3c-be0c-359bbd97381e",
        "subscription": "opt_out"
      }
     ]'
```

--------------------------------

### Update Contact Topics in JavaScript/TypeScript

Source: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/contacts/update-contact-topics

Use the Resend SDK to update contact topics by providing either a contact ID or email address.

```javascript
import { Resend } from 'resend';

const resend = new Resend('re_xxxxxxxxx');

// Update by contact id
const { data, error } = await resend.contacts.topics.update({
  id: 'e169aa45-1ecf-4183-9955-b1499d5701d3',
  topics: [
    {
      id: 'b6d24b8e-af0b-4c3c-be0c-359bbd97381e',
      subscription: 'opt_out',
    },
    {
      id: '07d84122-7224-4881-9c31-1c048e204602',
      subscription: 'opt_in',
    },
  ],
});

// Update by contact email
const { data, error } = await resend.contacts.topics.update({
  email: '[REDACTED_EMAIL]',
  topics: [
    {
      id: '07d84122-7224-4881-9c31-1c048e204602',
      subscription: 'opt_out',
    },
    {
      id: '07d84122-7224-4881-9c31-1c048e204602',
      subscription: 'opt_in',
    },
  ],
});
```

--------------------------------

### Resend::Contacts::Topics.list

Source: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/contacts/get-contact-topics

Retrieves a list of topics for a contact using the Resend Ruby SDK.

```APIDOC
## Resend::Contacts::Topics.list

### Description
Retrieves the topics associated with a specific contact. You can identify the contact by their unique ID or their email address.

### Method
Ruby SDK Method: `Resend::Contacts::Topics.list(id: string)`

### Parameters
- **id** (string) - Required - The unique identifier or email address of the contact.

### Usage Example
```ruby
require "resend"

Resend.api_key = "re_xxxxxxxxx"

# Get by contact id
contact_topics = Resend::Contacts::Topics.list(id: "e169aa45-1ecf-4183-9955-b1499d5701d3")

# Get by contact email
contact_topics = Resend::Contacts::Topics.list(id: "[REDACTED_EMAIL]")
```
```

### Add an unsubscribe link to transactional emails

Source: https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/emails/add-unsubscribe-to-transactional-emails

Resend does not manage contact lists for transactional emails. For workflows involving contact and unsubscribe management, users should utilize the Audiences feature, which is designed to track topics, segments, and unsubscribe preferences.

content.text:
### Customize Unsubscribe Link in Broadcast

Source: https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/segments/introduction

Use the RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL variable within your HTML template to provide a unique unsubscribe link for each recipient.

```json
"subject": "hello world",
"html": "Hi {{{contact.first_name|there}}}, you can unsubscribe here: {{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}}"
```

--------------------------------

### Add List-Unsubscribe Headers

Source: https://resend.com/blog/gmail-and-yahoo-bulk-sending-requirements-for-2024

Include these headers in your email configuration to enable the one-click unsubscribe mechanism required by Gmail and Yahoo.

```text
List-Unsubscribe: <https://example.com/unsubscribe>List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click
```

--------------------------------

### resend.broadcasts.create

Source: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/broadcasts/create-broadcast

Creates a new broadcast with the specified segment, sender, subject, content, and scheduling options.

```APIDOC
## resend.broadcasts.create

### Description
Creates a new broadcast to be sent to a specific segment of contacts. The broadcast can be sent immediately or scheduled for a future time.

### Parameters
- **segment_id** (string) - Required - The ID of the segment to receive the broadcast.
- **from** (string) - Required - The sender email address.
- **subject** (string) - Required - The subject line of the email.
- **html** (string) - Required - The HTML content of the email.
- **send** (boolean) - Optional - Whether to send the broadcast immediately.
- **scheduled_at** (string) - Optional - The time to schedule the broadcast (e.g., 'in 1 hour').

### Request Example
resend.broadcasts.create({
  'segment_id': '78261eea-8f8b-4381-83c6-79fa7120f1cf',
  'from': 'Acme <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>',
  'subject': 'hello world',
  'html': 'Hi {{{contact.first_name|there}}}, you can unsubscribe here: {{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}}',
  'send': true,
  'scheduled_at': 'in 1 hour'
});
```

### Knowledge Base > Should I add an unsubscribe link

Source: https://resend.com/docs/knowledge-base/should-i-add-an-unsubscribe-link

When using Resend Broadcasts or Automations, the platform can automatically manage unsubscribe requests. You can include the Unsubscribe Footer in your broadcasts or use a specific placeholder tag as a link target to customize the unsubscribe experience for your contacts.

--------------------------------

### Broadcasts > Handle unsubscribes

Source: https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/broadcasts/introduction

Resend automatically handles unsubscribe requests for your broadcasts. When a recipient clicks the unsubscribe link in an email, their subscription status is updated to ensure they no longer receive future communications from that broadcast list.

content.thinking:
I have enough to write up the recommendation now, following a design-review style with options, a clear recommendation, and trade-offs since this is an assessment rather than a code change. The current setup mirrors subscribers between MongoDB and Resend Audience, and sends the digest via batch send with individually rendered HTML per recipient.

Key gaps I'm noting: no List-Unsubscribe/List-Unsubscribe-Post headers (needed for Gmail/Yahoo one-click per RFC 8058), the unsubscribe endpoint is GET-only so it would 405 on POST; no idempotency keys on sends; no webhook handling for bounces/complaints so the DB and Resend can drift out of sync; the Audiences API is deprecated in favor of Segments though still functional; and the digest schedule field in the DB doesn't actually trigger anything since batch sends don't support scheduled_at.

My priority recommendation: keep the app's own subscriber store as the source of truth for privacy/deletion promises, but layer in Resend's native features — add List-Unsubscribe headers and a POST handler, use webhooks like contact.updated to reconcile deletions, and consider topic_id as a secondary safety net so Resend itself refuses sends to opted-out contacts.

Next I'm mapping out a webhook route that verifies signatures and handles bounces, complaints, and contact updates by deleting the subscriber record and removing them from contacts, plus adding idempotency keys for confirm and batch sends, and migrating from Audiences to the newer Segments API with a corresponding env variable rename.

I'm weighing whether to add an optional waitlist topic gate but deciding against it since it'd create a conflicting Resend-side state, and I'm ruling out Broadcasts entirely since their hosted unsubscribe only flags rather than deletes, contradicting the privacy promises already made, even though broadcasts would offer automatic List-Unsubscribe headers, scheduling, and analytics.

I'm also questioning whether the Resend contact mirror is even necessary at all — since suppressions for bounce/complaint tracking work independently of contacts, keeping a duplicate contact store only makes sense if Broadcasts or the dashboard are actually going to be used, otherwise dropping it reduces PII exposure and aligns better with data minimization.

content.text:
**Bottom line:** keep your own subscriber store as the source of truth. Resend has no "delete on unsubscribe" flow, so its hosted unsubscribe (Broadcasts, `{{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}}`, topic preference page) can never satisfy the privacy policy's "your address is then deleted" line on its own. But the current implementation leaves four things on the table that Resend does offer, and one of them is a real gap.

## What Resend offers vs. what you use

| Capability | Resend | You today |
|---|---|---|
| Unsubscribe headers on API sends | Not added automatically. Docs: "Resend does not manage contact lists for transactional emails"; you pass `List-Unsubscribe` + `List-Unsubscribe-Post` in `headers` | Not set. Only the footer link |
| Hosted unsubscribe / preference page | Broadcasts and `topic_id` only. Sets `unsubscribed: true` on the contact; never deletes | Correctly avoided |
| Bounce / complaint handling | Auto-suppression list plus webhooks `email.bounced`, `email.complained`, `email.suppressed`, `contact.updated` | No webhook route. Bounced or complaining addresses stay in Mongo forever |
| Idempotency keys | `{ idempotencyKey }` on single and batch sends, 24h window | Not used on confirm or digest sends |
| Audiences | Deprecated. SDK 6.28 marks `audienceId` `@deprecated`, use Segments | Still on `RESEND_AUDIENCE_ID` via the legacy overload |
| Scheduling | `scheduled_at` on single sends only, not batch | `digest schedule` writes a date to Mongo; nothing sends it |

## Recommended changes, in priority order

1. **Add one-click unsubscribe headers to the digest send** (`apps/email/scripts/digest.ts`). Gmail and Yahoo require RFC 8058 for bulk senders and show a native "Unsubscribe" button when the headers are present. Add per recipient:
   ```
   List-Unsubscribe: <https://hastoggle.dev/api/unsubscribe?token=...>
   List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click
   ```
   Then add a `POST` handler to `apps/web/app/api/unsubscribe/route.ts` that performs the same deletion and returns 200 with an empty body. Mail clients POST; today that would 405. Both handlers can share one function.

2. **Add a Resend webhook route** (e.g. `apps/web/app/api/webhooks/resend/route.ts`) verified with `resend.webhooks.verify`, handling `email.bounced` (permanent), `email.complained`, and `contact.updated` with `unsubscribed: true` by deleting the subscriber document and the contact. This is what makes "deleted, not parked" true even when the exit happens on Resend's side, and it stops the script re-sending to addresses Resend already suppresses. Needs a `RESEND_WEBHOOK_SECRET` key.

3. **Idempotency keys.** `confirm-email/<subscriberId>/<tokenHash>` on the confirmation send and `batch-digest/<digestId>` on the batch. Cheap, and the batch one prevents a double send if the script is re-run within 24h before the status flip lands.

4. **Decide the fate of the contact mirror.** It exists only to feed Broadcasts and the dashboard. If you are not going to use Broadcasts, drop `contacts.create` / `contacts.remove` and `RESEND_AUDIENCE_ID`: one fewer copy of the address, one fewer failure path, and suppression still works without contacts. If you keep it, migrate to Segments (`contacts.create({ email, segments: [{ id }] })`, `contacts.remove({ email })`, rename the env var to `RESEND_SEGMENT_ID`). My recommendation is drop it.

## Not recommended

- **Broadcasts for the digest.** You would get automatic headers, scheduling and analytics, but the hosted unsubscribe flags instead of deletes, so you would still need change 2 to honour the policy, and you lose the per-recipient token link the template enforces at the type level. Cohort waitlist volume does not justify it.
- **`topic_id` as a second gate.** Adds Resend-side subscription state that the Mongo query already governs, and its preference page contradicts the deletion promise.

Nothing here changes copy, so `docs/voice.md` is untouched. If you want, I can implement changes 1 to 3 as a PR with tests for the POST handler and the webhook route.

content.thinking:
I need to check the actual GDPR provisions here—Article 7(3) on withdrawing consent, Article 17 on the right to erasure and its exceptions like legal obligations or legal claims, plus Article 21(3) which covers objecting to direct marketing specifically.

Suppression lists are widely accepted as lawful (ICO, German DSK guidance) since keeping minimal data to honor opt-outs satisfies a legal obligation under Art. 6(1)(c)/(f) and Art. 21(3), plus UWG §7 in Germany. But I'm noting Resend's "unsubscribed: true" retains the entire contact record—names, properties, engagement data—which goes well beyond what a minimal suppression list requires, raising storage limitation and data minimization concerns under Art. 5(1)(e).

The cleaner legal path: since consent withdrawal removes the legal basis for the marketing profile under Art. 17(1)(b), that data should be deleted, while a minimal suppression entry (just an email or hash) persists under its own separate legal basis. So my conclusion is that GDPR doesn't require hard deletion on unsubscribe, but the current implementation—flipping a boolean while keeping the full profile—is weaker than best practice, and if the privacy policy promises deletion, that promise itself becomes binding.

**17(1)(a):** "the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed"

**17(1)(c):** "the data subject objects to the processing pursuant to Article 21(1) and there are no overriding legitimate grounds for the processing, or the data subject objects to the processing pursuant to Article 21(2)"

Based on the search results, here's what the ICO guidance says about direct marketing suppression lists and opt-out records:

## Maintaining Suppression Lists

Organizations should keep a 'do not contact' or suppression list of people who opt-out, unsubscribe or object to direct marketing. You should have a process in place to deal with anyone who tells you they no longer want your electronic mail marketing, and keep them on a suppression list.

## Legal Basis for Retention

A suppression list "supports the individual's right to object and is held for compliance rather than direct marketing purposes." This distinction is important under GDPR because it provides a lawful reason to retain personal data even after someone has requested deletion.

## Information to Keep

You should retain "just enough information to ensure that their preferences are respected in the future" - meaning you don't need to keep extensive personal data, just enough to process opt-out requests and honor their preferences.

## Handling Deletion Requests

If someone asks to delete their details, you should consider if it's appropriate to put a small amount of their information on your 'do not contact' list. This allows you to maintain compliance with both GDPR deletion rights and the practical need to respect opt-out preferences.

The key principle is that suppression lists serve a compliance function rather than a marketing function, which justifies keeping minimal identifying information despite a broader deletion request.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information from the DSK (Datenschutzkonferenz) Orientierungshilfe on direct marketing and data protection.

## Key Findings:

**Werbesperrdatei (Advertising Suppression List):**
If a person wants to prevent further advertising contact by a company, adding their contact data to an advertising suppression list at that company is the appropriate tool to consider. Such advertising suppression lists can be created under Article 21 Paragraph 3, Article 6 Paragraph 1 Sentence 1 lit. f GDPR in conjunction with Article 17 Paragraph 3 lit. b GDPR to account for advertising objections from affected persons.

**Widerspruch (Objection) Implementation:**
The implementation of an objection against future processing of contact data of an affected person for direct marketing purposes, including any associated profiling, must be carried out immediately by the respective company.

**Notification Requirements:**
Article 21 Paragraph 4 GDPR requires that the affected person be informed in clear and separate form of their right to object to processing of their personal data for direct marketing purposes including any associated profiling.

The Orientierungshilfe provides guidance on how companies must comply with GDPR requirements when processing personal data for direct marketing purposes, including proper handling of advertising objections and the use of suppression lists.

Der BGH hat mit Urteil vom 14. Januar 2016  - I ZR 65/14 - die Versendung von durch Facebook gene-

Einwilligung des Adressaten versandt werden. 
 
4.6 Zulässige Nutzungsdauer von Kontaktdaten der betroffenen Person für Zwecke der Direkt-
werbung 
 
Für zulässigerweise beim Betroffenen erhobene Kontaktdaten sieht das geltende Recht keine explizite 
Befristung einer werblichen Nutzung nach dem letzten aktiven Geschäfts - oder Direktwerbekontakt 
vor. Bei der Beurteilung, ab wann nach Art. 6 Abs. 1 UAbs. 1 lit. f DS-GVO überwiegende schutzwürdige 
Interessen der betroffenen Person einer länger währenden werblichen Nutzung entgegenstehen, 
sollte einerseits der Zeitablauf seit dem letzten aktiven Kontakt, andererseits die Art des Grundge-
schäfts berücksichtigt werden. 
 
Aufgrund der Art der Geschäftsbeziehung muss eine Erforderlichkeit zur weiteren Nutzung der Daten 
für Zwecke der Direktwerbung von dem V erantwortlichen nachvollziehbar dargelegt werden. Wenn 
nach einer langen „Werbepause“ die Kontaktdaten der Person plötzlich wieder für eine Werbezusen-
dung verarbeitet werden, dürfte dies bspw. für einen langjährigen Kundenstamm eher begründbar 
sein als für Kontakte, die lediglich aufgrund einer Konditionenabfrage angelegt worden sind.  
               
                        
 Seite 17 
 
Darüber hinaus können aber auch schon die Umstände des Erstkontakts einer Datennutzung für Wer-
bezwecke entgegenstehen. Dazu zählen wohl sämtliche von den Betroffenen als taktlos oder auf sons-
tige Weise unangemessen empfundene Werbeansprachen, insbesondere, wenn der Erstkontakt in ei-
ner akuten Ausnahmesituation zustande gekommen ist. So kann z. B. die Kontaktierung bzw. Inan-
spruchnahme eines Abschlepp - oder Schlüsselnotdienste s, einer Hebamme oder eines Bestatters 
keine längerfristige Datennutzung für werbliche Zwecke rechtfertigen. 
 
Im Rahmen der Interessenabwägung nach Art. 6 Abs. 1 UAbs. 1 lit. f DS-GVO sind zudem nach ErwGr 
47 DS-GVO die vernünftigen Erwartungen der betroffenen Personen, die auf ihrer Beziehung zu dem 
Verantwortlichen beruhen, zu berücksichtigen. Bei Berücksichtigung der Grundsätze aus Art. 5 Abs. 1 
DS-GVO ist offensichtlich, dass etwaige Erwartungen betroffener Person en, dass die von ihnen erho-
benen Daten für Direktwerbung genutzt werden, zeitlich nicht unbegrenzt sind. Der Zeitablauf ent-
scheidet daher mit über die Frage, ab wann die anfänglich nach Art. 6 Abs. 1 UAbs.  1 lit. f DS-GVO 
überwiegenden Werbeinteressen hinter die Interessen der betroffenen Person am Ausschluss einer 
werblichen Nutzung zurücktreten. 
 
5. Hinweise zu Art. 21 Abs. 2 bis 4 DS-GVO

Für die Umsetzung der Betroffenenrechte ist im Zweifelsfall von der betroffenen Person klarzustellen

I'm noting that GDPR Article 7(1) actually supports retaining a minimal proof-of-consent record (email, consent timestamp, withdrawal timestamp) for three years even after withdrawal, distinct from keeping the full marketing profile—which is the legally questionable part of just flipping a flag.

Resend's `unsubscribed: true` still retains first/last name, properties, and activity data at a US processor, so it's not the minimal compliant record either — keeping it for operational convenience would still require stripping the contact. My recommendation: keep deletion in Resend, optionally maintain a minimal consent-proof record in Mongo separately if re-subscribe protection matters, but honestly the current setup is already simplest and compliant unless Broadcasts is a real need.

content.text:
**Short answer: partly.** GDPR does not require hard deletion on unsubscribe as a general rule, but for a consent-based list like yours the "suppression list" justification does not apply, and Resend's `unsubscribed: true` flag is not the kind of retention the authorities accept. A soft-delete path is viable only if it is a minimal record you design, not Resend's flag.

## What the sources actually say

- **Art. 17(1)(b) GDPR:** erasure is required when "the data subject withdraws consent ... and where there is no other legal ground for the processing." So the question is whether another legal ground exists for what you keep.
- **ICO guidance (UK, persuasive not binding for you):** keep a suppression list holding "just enough information to ensure that their preferences are respected in the future"; it is "held for compliance rather than direct marketing purposes." This is the argument people usually cite for soft delete.
- **DSK Orientierungshilfe Direktwerbung (Feb 2022, your supervisory authorities), section 5.1:** a Werbesperrdatei is permitted under Art. 21(3), Art. 6(1)(f) with Art. 17(3)(b). But it adds the condition that kills the argument for you: "Eine Werbesperrdatei kann daher letztlich nur rechtmäßig sein, wenn die zu verhindernde Verarbeitung zu Werbezwecken auf Art. 6 Abs. 1 UAbs. 1 lit. f DS-GVO beruht." Your privacy policy states consent, Art. 6(1)(a). For consent-based marketing there is nothing to suppress, since you must hold a fresh consent before every send anyway.
- **DSK section 3.7 (withdrawal of consent):** on withdrawal "entfällt die Rechtsgrundlage für die weitere Verarbeitung," and the text assumes "Löschung der personenbezogenen Daten aus der Werbe-Datenbank." What the controller may keep is proof that consent existed, for 3 years, under Art. 6(1)(c) and (f), and this continued retention must be disclosed at collection time.

## What this means for the design

| Option | Compliant? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Current: delete Mongo doc and Resend contact | Yes | Strictly, you are slightly under-retaining: you keep no proof of consent, which the DSK expects for 3 years |
| Resend `unsubscribed: true`, keep the contact | Not defensibly | Keeps email, names, properties and engagement events at a US processor with no legal ground after withdrawal. Data minimisation and storage limitation both cut against it |
| Minimal consent record in Mongo, delete everything else | Yes, and arguably better than today | Email (or a hash plus timestamp), consented-at, withdrawn-at, confirmation IP if you log it. Must be disclosed in the privacy policy before signup |

So the viable soft-delete path is the third row, and it is a Mongo change, not a Resend one. The Resend contact should still be removed on unsubscribe, which is what the route already does. The privacy policy would need two edits: replace "your address is then deleted from the list" with wording that a consent record is retained for three years, and add that to the retention section.

**Recommendation:** keep the deletion contract as is, and add the consent record only if you actually want the proof or a re-subscribe guard. Do not adopt Resend's flag for it. Whichever way you go, the unsubscribe headers and the webhook from the earlier plan stand.

Sources: [gdpr-info.eu Art. 17](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/), [ICO: Respect people's preferences](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/direct-marketing-guidance/respect-peoples-preferences/), [ICO direct marketing checklist](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/direct-marketing-checklist/), [DSK Orientierungshilfe Werbung, Februar 2022 (PDF)](https://www.datenschutzkonferenz-online.de/media/oh/OH-Werbung_Februar%202022_final.pdf), [LDI NRW on the Orientierungshilfe](https://www.ldi.nrw.de/datenschutz-und-direktwerbung-neue-orientierungshilfe).

content.thinking: Article 3(1) applies since Eric's establishment in Osnabrück is the controller, so GDPR covers all users worldwide regardless of where processing occurs—Article 3(2) is the reverse case for non-EU controllers targeting EU subjects. Other jurisdictions' laws, like CAN-SPAM for US recipients, could apply on top of this.

content.text:
**All users.** GDPR attaches to the controller, not the data subject's location. Art. 3(1) applies the regulation to "processing of personal data in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or a processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing takes place in the Union or not." hasToggle is established in Osnabrück, so every subscriber, wherever they are, is covered. Recital 22 confirms that establishment means "the effective and real exercise of activity through stable arrangements," which a sole proprietor's business address satisfies.

Art. 3(2) is the other direction: it pulls non-EU controllers into scope when they target people in the EU. It is not a limiter on you.

Two practical consequences:

- **Design once.** The deletion or consent-record rule from the last answer applies uniformly. There is no reason to branch on recipient country.
- **Other laws stack on top, they never subtract.** US recipients also bring CAN-SPAM (opt-out honoured within 10 business days, physical address in the footer, which you already have), Canadian ones CASL, UK ones UK GDPR plus PECR. All are satisfied by the stricter GDPR path, so nothing extra is needed for the waitlist.

# Automations

## Overview

Automations are event-driven workflows composed of steps connected in a directed graph. Each automation has a trigger step that starts the flow, followed by action steps (send email, delay, wait for event, condition, contact update, contact delete, add to segment).

Automations are created in a `disabled` state by default. Set `status: "enabled"` to activate.

## SDK Methods

### Node.js

| Operation | Method | Notes |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| Create | `resend.automations.create(params)` | Returns automation ID |
| Get | `resend.automations.get(id)` | Returns full automation with steps and connections |
| List | `resend.automations.list(params?)` | Filter by `status`, cursor-paginated |
| Update | `resend.automations.update(params)` | Partial update — name, status, or steps+connections |
| Delete | `resend.automations.remove(id)` | Permanent |
| Stop | `resend.automations.stop(id)` | Sets status to `disabled` |
| List Runs | `resend.automations.runs.list({ automationId, status? })` | Filter by run status |
| Get Run | `resend.automations.runs.get({ automationId, runId })` | Returns run with executed steps |

### Python

`resend.Automations.create/get/list/update/remove/stop` — same operations with snake_case params.

## Graph Model

An automation is a directed graph of **steps** connected by **connections**.

content.text:
**Segments are just named contact lists** (contacts are now global, a contact can sit in several segments, and the old Audience is a segment with a legacy alias). **Broadcasts are campaigns sent to a segment**, composed in the dashboard editor or created via the API with `html` / `react`, then sent or scheduled. Automations sit on top: event-triggered flows such as "contact created, wait 2 days, send email."

What dropping the contact mirror costs you, ranked by how much I think it matters for the waitlist:

| Lost | What it actually is | Do you need it? |
|---|---|---|
| Dashboard send | Write a cohort announcement in Resend's editor, pick the segment, hit send. No `bun digest` script, no deploy | The one real loss. Today every send needs a terminal and Mongo access |
| Automatic unsubscribe plumbing | `{{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}}`, one-click headers, hosted preference page, unsubscribed and suppressed contacts skipped automatically | Only useful if you accept the flag-not-delete model, which we ruled out |
| Per-campaign analytics | Delivered, opened, clicked, unsubscribed rates per broadcast in the dashboard | Nice to have. Batch sends still show per-email events in the Emails tab and via webhooks |
| Scheduling that sends | `scheduledAt` on a broadcast, cancel reverts to draft | Your `digest schedule` command only writes a date and nothing sends it. A broadcast would close that gap |
| Personalisation variables | `{{{contact.first_name\|there}}}` and custom properties | You collect only an email |
| Topics | Per-category opt-in and opt-out | One list, one topic. Not needed |
| Automations | Welcome sequences, delay, conditions, add-to-segment | Could replace the confirmation email flow, but you need double opt-in with your own token, which Automations cannot do |
| Contact export and dashboard visibility | See the list in Resend, export CSV | Mongo has the same data |

So the trade is: **the dashboard send and scheduling** versus **the deletion promise and the per-recipient token link**. Everything else is either irrelevant at one topic and one field, or reproducible with the webhook route.

If the dashboard send is what you would miss, there is a middle path: keep the Resend contact mirror and the webhook from the earlier plan, send announcements as Broadcasts with `{{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}}`, and let the `contact.updated` webhook turn Resend's flag into a Mongo deletion plus `contacts.remove`. Resend still holds the address between the click and the webhook, which is seconds, and the privacy policy stays true. You lose the compile-time guarantee on the unsubscribe link and take a dependency on webhook delivery for the promise.

My recommendation stands: drop the mirror now, ship headers, webhook and idempotency. Revisit Broadcasts when sends stop being rare enough for a script.

content.thinking:
There's some inconsistency on the rate limit figure—some sources say 2 requests per second by default, others reference 10. I should mention both possibilities and point to the ratelimit headers (limit, remaining, retry-after) as the authoritative source.

The bigger issue is a real bug: batch sending over 100 recipients will fail validation since Resend batches are atomic and capped at 100. I need to chunk into groups of 100, throttle to the rate limit, use per-chunk idempotency keys, retry on 429 honoring retry-after, and persist progress per chunk so reruns can resume—also worth flagging the free plan's daily 100-email cap and domain warm-up considerations, since broadcasts don't apply here at all.

content.text:
**Today's script breaks at 101 recipients.** `resend.batch.send` accepts at most 100 emails per call and is atomic, so a single call with the whole list fails validation and nothing goes out. Rate limits are the smaller problem.

The facts:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Emails per batch call | 100, max 50 recipients each, no attachments or scheduling |
| API requests per second | Docs currently say 10 per team, older docs and the skill say 2. Read the `ratelimit-limit` and `ratelimit-remaining` response headers to know yours |
| Over the limit | 429 with a `retry-after` header |
| Free plan | 100 emails per day. Pro and up have no daily cap |
| New domain warm-up | Roughly 150 on day one, ramping over about two weeks |

What the script needs to send to many contacts yourself:

1. **Chunk into 100s** and send sequentially, one chunk per request. Even at 2 requests per second that is 10,000 emails in under a minute, so throughput is not the concern.
2. **Idempotency key per chunk**, e.g. `batch-digest/<digestId>/<chunkIndex>`. A re-run inside 24 hours returns the original response instead of double-sending.
3. **Retry 429 and 5xx** with backoff that honours `retry-after`. Do not retry 4xx validation errors.
4. **Record progress per chunk in Mongo**, not one `sentAt` at the end. A crash at chunk 7 of 12 must resume at 8, and the idempotency keys make the resume safe even if the record is stale.
5. **Skip bounced and complained addresses before building chunks.** Resend suppresses them anyway, but the webhook route from the earlier plan is what keeps them out of your list.

All of this is about 40 lines in `apps/email/scripts/digest.ts`, and it is exactly the work Broadcasts does for you. With a broadcast you hand Resend the segment and it owns fan-out, throttling, retries, suppression and warm-up pacing. That is the strongest argument for Broadcasts in this whole thread, stronger than the dashboard editor.

So the decision reframes to list size. Below a few thousand confirmed addresses, the chunked script is fine and keeps the deletion contract simple. If you expect the waitlist to grow past that, the middle path from the last answer, Broadcasts plus the `contact.updated` webhook that converts Resend's flag into a deletion, is the one I would build.

No blocking reason. My hesitation was scope, not compliance: the waitlist is small today and the chunked script is less surface. But you are right that the middle path is inside the GDPR posture, and the webhook and Segments migration are work I already recommended. Building Broadcasts on top is the incremental part.

One honest caveat before the plan. The deletion promise would then depend on webhook delivery. Resend retries failed webhooks for about a day, and an unsubscribed contact is never sent to in the meantime, so no email leaks. But if the endpoint is down long enough, Resend keeps the address until a reconciliation pass runs. A nightly job that lists contacts with `unsubscribed: true` and deletes them closes that hole. I would include it.

## Proposal

1. **Segments.** Replace `audienceId` with `segments: [{ id }]` on create, `contacts.remove({ email })` on delete. Rename the env var to `RESEND_SEGMENT_ID`. The existing audience id keeps working as the segment id.
2. **Webhook route** at `apps/web/app/api/webhooks/resend/route.ts`, verified with `resend.webhooks.verify`. On `contact.updated` with `unsubscribed: true`, `email.bounced` (permanent) and `email.complained`: delete the Mongo row and the Resend contact. New env var `RESEND_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Tests for signature rejection and each event.
3. **Digest becomes a broadcast.** `bun digest send` calls `broadcasts.create` with `react: DigestEmail(...)` and `segmentId`, then `broadcasts.send`. `digest schedule` passes `scheduledAt`, so scheduling finally sends. The template's required `unsubscribeUrl` receives the `{{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}}` placeholder, and a test asserts the rendered HTML contains it. One-click headers come from Resend.
4. **Keep `/api/unsubscribe`.** Older digests carry token links. Add the `POST` handler anyway so those links satisfy one-click too.
5. **Reconciliation** as a cron in `apps/api/app/cron/` or a script command, deleting any contact Resend has flagged.
6. **Idempotency keys** on the confirmation send.
7. **Privacy policy.** No promise changes. One factual edit: Resend now holds the address between click and webhook, which the current text already covers by naming Resend as processor.

Out of scope: dashboard-composed broadcasts work automatically once the segment exists, no code needed. Topics and Automations stay unused.

Rough size: one PR, about a dozen files, tests for the webhook route and the broadcast payload. Manual steps on your side afterwards: create the webhook in the Resend dashboard pointing at the production URL and copy the secret into Vercel.

Say yes and I will build it on this branch.

content.thinking:
I see two issues to fix: the digest.ts insertOne call needs an explicit `_id: new ObjectId()` since TypeScript's OptionalUnlessRequiredId isn't inferring it as optional, and Biome is flagging async functions without await in test mocks plus import sorting problems.

For the reconcile test's unexpected 401, I'm tracing through why the env mock might not be applying — the route imports `@/env` directly, and since path-alias mocks are unreliable in preload, the real env.ts likely loads and reads `process.env.RECONCILE_SECRET` normally. I need to actually debug this by logging values rather than reasoning through it further.

Actually, I think I've found the real culprit: Bun runs all test files in a single process, so `mock.module` calls are global, not scoped per file. My per-file override of `@repo/database` in the reconcile/webhook tests is leaking into other test files, breaking things like the confirm test's `createId` import, and likely causing the 401 too. The fix is to avoid re-mocking `@repo/database` per file and instead have the preload's mock delegate to a mutable object on `globalThis`, or have tests use `spyOn` on the preload-mocked module's exports instead of calling `mock.module` again.

Since the mock object identity persists across imports, I can spy directly on methods like `subscriber.deleteOne` or `resend.webhooks.verify` and restore them after each test rather than replacing the whole module. Time to rewrite both test files using this spyOn approach and apply all the fixes.

feat(email): digests go out as Resend broadcasts; exits still delete

The waitlist keeps its privacy promise — an unsubscribed address is
deleted, not parked — while handing fan-out to Resend. Broadcasts send to
the segment, skip unsubscribed and suppressed contacts, pace the send,
and substitute each recipient's unsubscribe link for the placeholder the
template now carries. Resend's link only flips the contact's
`unsubscribed` flag, so a verified webhook at /api/webhooks/resend turns
that flag — and permanent bounces, complaints and dashboard deletions —
into the deletion in both stores. Behind it, POST /api/reconcile (bearer
token, meant for a scheduled Atlas trigger) sweeps whatever the webhook
missed and drops signups whose confirmation link has been dead a week.

Verified against the DSK Orientierungshilfe Direktwerbung: for a
consent-based list the suppression-list exception does not apply, so the
deletion contract stays and Resend's soft flag alone would not do.

The per-subscriber unsubscribe token, its route and /unsubscribed go —
no digest ever carried one. Audiences become segments
(RESEND_AUDIENCE_ID → RESEND_SEGMENT_ID), the confirmation send carries
an idempotency key, and `digest schedule` finally sends: a future date is
passed to Resend as the broadcast's scheduledAt.

Verified: 260 web tests, 2 email package tests, typecheck across web,
app, email, @repo/email, @repo/database, Biome clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

name: resend-unsubscribe-model
description: 2026-09-14 decision — digests are Resend broadcasts, but unsubscribe still deletes (webhook + Atlas reconcile); GDPR verification says soft flag alone is not enough for a consent-based list

On 2026-09-14 Eric approved the "middle path" for the waitlist email stack: Resend Broadcasts to a Segment for sending, with `/api/webhooks/resend` turning Resend's `unsubscribed` flag (plus permanent bounces, complaints, dashboard deletions) into a deletion in both Mongo and Resend, and `POST /api/reconcile` (bearer `RECONCILE_SECRET`) as the safety net, called by a MongoDB Atlas scheduled trigger that Eric builds himself using Atlas Values.

**Why:** Eric asked whether GDPR lets him loosen "your address is then deleted" to Resend's soft flag. Verified against the DSK Orientierungshilfe Direktwerbung (Feb 2022, §5.1 and §3.7): a Werbesperrdatei is only lawful when the marketing rests on Art. 6(1)(f); hasToggle's list is consent-based (Art. 6(1)(a)), so on withdrawal the marketing data must go, and only a minimal consent-proof record could be kept (3 years, must be disclosed at collection). Resend's flag keeps the whole contact at a US processor, so it is not that record. GDPR applies to all subscribers worldwide because the controller is established in the EU (Art. 3(1)).

**How to apply:** Never propose Resend's hosted unsubscribe or Topics preference page as the end state on its own. Any new exit path (new webhook event, new list) must call `removeSubscriber` in `apps/web/lib/subscribers.ts`. The privacy policy's deletion sentence stays true and must not be softened. See [[hastoggle-positioning]] for the waitlist framing.
